common_name: Mango Tango Agastache (Vivid Orange-Red Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential for winter survival, since agastache crowns rot readily in wet, heavy soil.

directions: Mango Tango carries dense, tightly packed flower spikes in a vivid orange-red over aromatic, gray-green, anise-scented foliage, one of the warmest, most saturated colors available among hardy hummingbird mints. It blooms continuously from early summer into fall on an upright, self-supporting plant that needs no staking, drawing hummingbirds, bumble bees, and butterflies heavily throughout its long bloom season. Give it lean, sharply drained soil and full sun, the same conditions its dryland-adapted relatives need, and leave the seed heads standing through winter both for extra garden interest and as a food source for finches.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; like other Gaillardia, Burgundy is short-lived in heavy, wet soil, so sharp drainage matters more than fertility for long-term survival.

directions: Burgundy is an older, long-grown Gaillardia selection valued for its unusually solid, deep wine-red ray petals, lacking the yellow tips typical of most blanket flower cultivars, which gives it a richer, more uniform color for a border or cutting garden. Like other Gaillardia x grandiflora selections it produces a long succession of single, daisy-form flowers with a domed central cone from late spring through fall, drawing bees and butterflies throughout the season, and its native prairie parentage gives it strong heat and drought tolerance. Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun, and deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom, or leave some heads to set seed if self-sown volunteers are welcome in the bed.

common_name: Mesa Peach Blanket Flower (Compact Soft Peach Gaillardia)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Mesa Peach was bred as a seed-grown, first-year-flowering selection, so an early start gives the longest bloom season.

directions: Mesa Peach is an All-America Selections winner notable as the first blanket flower bred with a soft, unusual peach-and-cream color, a gentle pastel departure from the hot red-and-yellow tones typical of the species, on a compact, non-flopping mound that stays under 14 inches tall. Like Arizona Sun in the same Mesa series, it flowers heavily and continuously from its first season through frost, is seed-grown for uniform, reliable garden performance, and draws bees and butterflies over its long bloom season. Give it the same lean, sharply drained, sandy soil and full sun that all Gaillardia demand, since wet, heavy soil is the most common cause of crown rot and premature decline.

common_name: Supreme Cantaloupe Coneflower (Double Proliferous Orange Echinacea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Supreme Cantaloupe's fully double flowers are produced on strong stems that hold up well without staking in a typical border.

directions: Supreme Cantaloupe carries fully double, pompom-like flowers in a warm cantaloupe-orange, the disc florets multiplying into a rounded, ruffled center instead of the flat cone typical of species coneflower, on sturdy, well-branched stems. It blooms over a long stretch from early summer into fall and, despite the doubled flower form that reduces the exposed pollen and nectar somewhat compared to single-flowered coneflowers, still draws bees and butterflies steadily through the season. Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring, and deadhead spent flowers to keep the display going, since doubled coneflower cultivars set less viable seed than single forms and rely more on division for propagation.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
